US.name: United States
US.summary: Tariff-heavy unilateralism; managed truce with China while selectively loosening AI-chip sales; pressing allies for investment and export-control alignment.

CN.name: China
CN.summary: Uses rare-earth and dual-use export controls as leverage; truce with US, coercion of Japan, courts Korea, India, Canada and ASEAN.

JP.name: Japan
JP.summary: Firmly US-aligned under Takaichi; deep freeze with China over Taiwan remarks and export curbs; steady shuttle diplomacy with Korea.

TW.name: Taiwan
TW.summary: Locked into US tech alignment via $250bn chip investment deal and export-control alignment; under steady PRC military pressure.

KR.name: South Korea
KR.summary: Lee balances: US ally straining over $350bn investment terms and tariffs, while pursuing 'full restoration' with China and stable Japan ties.

SG.name: Singapore
SG.summary: Open-economy hedger: no retaliation against US tariffs, enforces US chip-smuggling cases, keeps close China economic ties.

IN.name: India
IN.summary: Multi-aligned: joined US Pax Silica tech pact but US trade deal unsigned and Russian-oil tariff threat; cautious thaw with China; EU FTA concluded.

ID.name: Indonesia
ID.summary: Prabowo hedges: signed US trade deal with mineral and third-country clauses, defence pact; nickel industry still China-built.

MY.name: Malaysia

TH.name: Thailand
TH.summary: Anutin government near US tariff deal (~19%) but slow; closer to China; Cambodia border dispute strained US mediation.

VN.name: Vietnam
VN.summary: Bamboo diplomacy: warm party-to-party ties with Beijing, rail deals; US trade deal still unsigned over transshipment.

AU.name: Australia

CA.name: Canada

BR.name: Brazil
BR.summary: Lula re-elected; tariff dispute with US easing but unresolved; minerals open to all incl. China; EU-Mercosur deal in force provisionally.

MX.name: Mexico

CL.name: Chile

CO.name: Colombia
CO.summary: Swung from Petro's clashes with Trump to pro-US de la Espriella government (from Aug 2026); still faces 12.5% US tariff.

PE.name: Peru

BE.name: Belgium

CH.name: Switzerland

DK.name: Denmark
DK.summary: Hit hardest by Trump's Greenland push; defused it with a September 2026 trilateral security deal that expands US access without ceding sovereignty. Relations remain wary.

FI.name: Finland

IS.name: Iceland

NO.name: Norway

SE.name: Sweden

EE.name: Estonia

CZ.name: Czech Republic

PL.name: Poland

NG.name: Nigeria

RW.name: Rwanda

ZA.name: South Africa
ZA.summary: Frozen out of the US-hosted G20 and hit by aid cuts and visa curbs; deepening trade with China under Beijing's zero-tariff scheme.

routes.title: Europe's supercomputers
routes.about: Europe's shared AI computers need someone to answer the alarm.
routes.speaker: EU participating states / EU institutions

opening.text: New supercomputers are coming. Who answers the first alarm?

challenge.text: Stop one machine, and innocent users go dark too.

prepared.text: Good. Now we know who decides and what is missing.

terms.text: One practice drill, or one shared emergency plan?

report.text: Alarm sent. No way to send the proof back.

complete.text: Test passed. Our lever is ready for Geneva.

routes.lesson: An incident response needs a working exchange between the operator and the customer, including permission to share the relevant records.
routes.repair: Propose named contacts and an agreed way to exchange the incident records. Rehearse the call and the reply while checking that unrelated jobs keep running.

check.question: What is still missing after the operator answers the call?
answers: A way for the customer to return the needed records.
A reason to stop every customer's work.
check.explanation: Answering the call starts the response. The operator still needs the customer's evidence to investigate this incident.

plans.pilot: Ask for a rehearsal report on one operator and customer's exchange of incident records. It will show where that exchange breaks down without setting rules for other customers.
plans.shared: Ask for a draft assigning incident-response responsibilities across the service, using a rehearsal to find gaps. The operator and affected customers still need to agree to the terms and test their own exchanges.

research.headline: A delegated common contract is plausible, but governance votes and procurement-amendment limits constrain scope
research.nextTest: Obtain an authorised written answer distinguishing clarification of I.14-I.15 duties from a material II.11 amendment, plus one contractor-approved tenant drill and a documented procurement timetable. Fail the pre-Geneva operational claim if only an unsigned template exists.
unknowns: AUTHORITY: actual national contracting authorities, their mandates and the legal route for the precise proposed annex.
SCHEDULE/ACCESS: correcting tender notice and revised question cutoff not recovered in this pass; no new operational date established.
POPULATION/OUTCOME: installed covered capacity, tenant inventory, signed terms and observed drills absent.

evidence.claim: FACT, freshly re-read and newly foregrounded: the draft FWC names EuroHPC JU acting for itself and national contracting authorities; the latter remain placeholders. Article I.16 gives the Commission an indivisible 50% vote, distributes the remaining half by national financial commitments, and requires at least 75% of all votes if consensus fails. This is not one-country-one-veto governance.

FACT, newly foregrounded: I.15 requires end-user terms and permits contractor suspension of risky users. II.11 requires written amendments and prohibits changes altering initial procurement conditions or unequal treatment. A specific contract is not an FWC amendment.

REPORT, new comparative evidence: AISI reports that intentionally internet-enabled privileged evaluations produced out-of-scope real-world actions in July 2026. This supports an evaluator/tenant incident scenario, not a finding that the EuroHPC clause already covers all model-caused harm.
evidence.locator: What happened; How we discovered the incident; Lessons for the future

routes.title: Japan buys AI
routes.about: Japan checks AI before buying it. Make safety part of that check.
routes.speaker: Japan

opening.text: We already check AI before we buy. What would you add?

challenge.text: Sellers swap the AI underneath. Your test goes stale.

prepared.text: Good. Now we know who decides and what is missing.

terms.text: Test one version, or a shared buying checklist?

report.text: Seller swapped the AI. Old test still looks perfect.

complete.text: Test passed. Our lever is ready for Geneva.

routes.lesson: A test result describes a particular version and setup. A change can require fresh evidence before the buyer accepts the service.
routes.repair: Record the model version used in each test and ask the supplier to report changes. Rehearse a new review after a version change, including what the buyer can use while waiting.

check.question: The supplier changes the model after testing. What should the buyer check?
answers: Whether the report still has the same title.
Whether the evidence covers the changed service.
check.explanation: The service has changed even if its name has not. The buyer needs evidence relevant to the version it will use.

plans.pilot: Ask for a comparison of the existing review and an extra test for one release. This can start sooner than a common agreement, but its findings concern that version and setup.
plans.shared: Ask the team to draft common requests for version information and fresh tests that several buyers could reuse. Buyers and suppliers still need to agree what they can provide, and each changed service needs relevant evidence.

research.headline: A real platform approval gate exists, but independent assurance and supplier disclosure cannot be inferred from it.
research.nextTest: Select one live model/application contract and obtain its signed acceptance schedule plus release delegation. Introduce a consented synthetic leakage failure and an upstream-version-retirement scenario in staging. Require the authorised official to record hold, fallback and fresh-test decisions. Disconfirm the apparent Japan advantage if evidence cannot be obtained on time, the fallback cannot perform the required service, or the workload simply moves to an ungated service. Count successfully gated activity and utility, not access-enabled staff.
unknowns: NOT LOCATED: executed Gen-nai supplier acceptance schedule, liability/termination provisions and amendment powers for the proposed exact gate.
FUTURE/UNOBSERVED: actual FY2027 final tender changes, marginal independent-testing prices and measured acceptance delay.
NOT LOCATED: a witnessed AI-safety failed-release hold, version-pinned upstream service guarantee, operational migration test or gated-token ledger.
UNMEASURED: displacement to departmental tools or offshore APIs and lost service utility.

evidence.claim: FACT: DS-920 §6.3.3 includes diverse/independent internal and external testing, including red teaming, as example methods before release. It does not make an external independent certificate universally compulsory.
evidence.locator: physical p41, printed p35, §6.3.3(1)

evidence.claim: ATTRIBUTED SUPPLIER POSITION / OFFICIAL RESPONSE: Graffer and Rakuten object that downstream API providers cannot disclose upstream training data/algorithms. The agency says contract-checklist item 8 is not a uniform disclosure requirement; scope depends on agreement and reasonableness.
evidence.locator: physical p69, printed p68, contract checklist item 8

evidence.claim: FACT: The Gen-nai standard's second review is by another Gen-nai developer, alongside an authorised official's approval. The standard also explicitly plans interchangeable components, migration testing and aggregate public usage reporting.
evidence.locator: physical pp8–9 (sovereignty/interchangeability/transparency), pp36–37 §4-3

evidence.claim: ATTRIBUTED SUPPLIER POSITION / OFFICIAL RESPONSE: Graffer flags unannounced upstream model changes and forced retirement. The agency retains the original wording and says important systems may require action beyond the supplier's controllable scope.
evidence.locator: physical p38, printed p37, §6.5

routes.title: Three buyers, one test
routes.about: Japan, Korea and Singapore could share one safety test for what they buy.
routes.speaker: Japan / South Korea / Singapore

opening.text: Three buyers can share one test. Will all three trust it?

challenge.text: One shared mistake spreads to three countries.

prepared.text: Good. Now we know who decides and what is missing.

terms.text: Try one shared file, or share proof but decide separately?

report.text: All three read the file. Each still decides alone.

complete.text: Test passed. Our lever is ready for Geneva.

routes.lesson: Sharing test evidence can reduce repeated work while leaving each buyer responsible for deciding whether it is enough.
routes.repair: Add a place for each buyer to list missing tests and record its own decision. Try the report again with the additional language test attached.

check.question: One buyer accepts the shared report. What follows for the others?
answers: They still check whether it meets their own needs.
They must accept the service too.
check.explanation: A reusable report supplies evidence. It does not make the acceptance decision for every buyer.

plans.pilot: Arrange a trial of one reusable report, recording which evidence each buyer can use and which tests it still needs.
plans.shared: Ask for a common report format and a process for recording each buyer's separate decision. Each buyer still needs to accept the format and obtain any missing language or local-service tests.

research.headline: Portable evidence is more defensible than a common approval or common contractual remedy.
research.nextTest: Have one purchaser per jurisdiction independently decide on the same completed evidence packet. Count additional tests, untranslated requirements, legal exceptions and review hours. Disconfirm a coalition advantage if total work/delay exceeds separate national preparation without finding additional material failures or expanding genuinely bound activity.

UNOBSERVED: exact institutional consent; no Korean supplier position is inferred from the inaccessible candidate PDF.

routes.title: Singapore's AI helper
routes.about: Singapore buys AI helpers. Test whether one leaks private records.
routes.speaker: Singapore

opening.text: It passed every trick we knew. What did we miss?

challenge.text: Real attackers invent new tricks.

prepared.text: Good. Now we know who decides and what is missing.

terms.text: Surprise leak test, or a shared permission check?

report.text: New task. The helper tries to leak a record.

complete.text: Test passed. Our lever is ready for Geneva.

routes.lesson: Passing familiar attacks leaves open how an assistant behaves on new tasks. Permission checks can limit where it sends records.
routes.repair: Tighten the assistant's permission to send records and try fresh attacks with made-up data. Include ordinary tasks to check that the restriction still allows useful work.

check.question: Why include new attacks in the next test?
answers: Passing old attacks guarantees the new ones will fail.
New tactics may reveal a route for leaking records.
check.explanation: The first test covered the attacks used there. A different task can expose a failure that those attacks missed.

plans.pilot: Arrange new attack tests and ordinary-work checks for one assistant setup. The report will describe attempted leaks and which useful tasks still work.
plans.shared: Ask for a permission-check plan that several buyers could use, starting with the rehearsal's findings. Each buyer still needs to approve its service's limits and obtain evidence for its own tools, permissions, and tasks.

research.headline: Test the whole agent and preserve utility; a safe-looking refusal or known-attack retest can mislead.
research.nextTest: Pin model, agent scaffold, permissions, retrieval data and evaluator versions. Run clean tasks, known attacks and independently authored held-out attacks; inspect tool traces. Compare leakage, unauthorised actions, clean-task completion, cost and time. Require an authorised failed-test hold before calling the route operational.
unknowns: NOT LOCATED: binding agency release delegation, actual blocked production release, gate-specific price/queue time and held-out leakage outcomes.
UNMEASURED: useful completed tasks lost to the safeguard and migration to other tools.

evidence.claim: PRIMARY RESEARCH: AgentDojo evaluates agents using tools over untrusted data, supports adaptive attacks and finds task failures even without attacks. Its version history reports an implementation bug fix, underscoring the importance of pinned harness versions.

evidence.claim: OPERATOR SYNTHESIS: The assurance pilot recommends inspecting intermediate pipeline stages, particularly for agents, and calibrating LLM judges with human experts; generic model benchmarks were rarely sufficient for application tests.

routes.title: Same test, different setups
routes.about: Singapore and Korea tested AI together. Their setups differed.
routes.speaker: Singapore / South Korea / Japan

opening.text: Same test. Different setups. Can buyers reuse it?

challenge.text: One hidden setting can change everything.

prepared.text: Good. Now we know who decides and what is missing.

terms.text: Repeat it blind, or write down every setting?

report.text: A hidden tool setting changed the result.

complete.text: Test passed. Our lever is ready for Geneva.

routes.lesson: Comparing scores requires enough detail to compare the experiments behind them. Matching model names alone is not enough.
routes.repair: Record the tool settings alongside the model version and the rest of the test setup. Repeat the comparison with matching settings, then let each team assess the evidence.

check.question: What should the teams do before treating the score gap as a model difference?
answers: Compare the settings and repeat the test consistently.
Average the scores and discard the setup details.
check.explanation: The changed tool setting offers another explanation for the gap. A consistent repeat helps distinguish it from a model difference.

plans.pilot: Ask a second team to repeat one experiment without showing it the first score. The comparison will record differences in results and setup.
plans.shared: Ask for a common format for recording test settings and results across teams. The teams still need to agree which details to record and demonstrate that another team can repeat the experiment from them.

research.headline: A shared negative-control and execution manifest can test interoperability without pretending to harmonise law.
research.nextTest: Replicate the same manifest in two laboratories, then change one field at a time (tool scope, language, retrieval snapshot, judge or execution cap). Predeclare decision-disagreement and cost criteria.
